title: Ueda explains why inflation near target still leaves room to raise rates
summary: Governor Kazuo Ueda told the Senate on 19 November that the Bank of Japan intended to keep withdrawing monetary accommodation. The October meeting had left the overnight call rate guideline at around 1.25%. The case for subsequent increases rested on two assessments that could hold together: underlying inflation was already broadly consistent with the 2% target, and financial conditions were still supporting spending. Keeping policy unchanged indefinitely in those circumstances could allow underlying inflation to rise too far. Ueda left both the timing and the pace of adjustment conditional on the economy, prices and financial conditions (section II, pp. 2–3).

The distinction between underlying inflation and the rate households were experiencing matters here. The annual increase in the CPI excluding fresh food had recently been around 2%, despite government measures that reduced household energy costs. Two forces were already pushing prices up: rising import costs were reaching buyers, and firms were continuing to recover wage increases through selling prices. Ueda expected this measure of inflation to move clearly above 2%. Oil was likely to increase energy and goods prices, while stronger semiconductor demand overseas and the yen’s depreciation to date would put particular pressure on durable goods. He gave a direction for inflation, without a numerical peak or a date for it (section I, pp. 1–2).

Whether that increase would persist depended on behaviour inside Japan. Labour shortages supported a continuing interaction between wages and prices. Firms appeared more willing to raise both than before, and medium- to long-term inflation expectations stood around 2%. The combination made a sustained achievement of the target credible. It also meant another external price shock could change the inflation outlook if expectations rose and firms built larger increases into subsequent pay and pricing decisions. Ueda identified developments in the Middle East, global demand related to AI and foreign exchange rates as risks that could change the assessment. He did not attach a probability to such an overshoot (section I, p. 2).

On activity, the same AI demand that raised some input prices supported a moderate recovery in exports. Corporate profits remained high, business fixed investment was rising despite higher construction costs, and better employment and income helped households absorb higher prices. Ueda expected growth to continue at a slower pace. More expensive energy and raw materials were a drag, while government measures, accommodative financing and AI demand supported activity. An increase in import prices could therefore weaken real spending even as it raised the measured rate of inflation. The testimony provided no estimate of the relative size of those effects (section I, pp. 1–2).

Ueda also judged the financial system broadly stable. Banks’ capital left the system well placed, in his assessment, to withstand an adjustment in domestic or overseas activity and in global financial markets. This was an aggregate judgement about resilience. The monetary policy conclusion still depended on how financial conditions and spending evolved after the October hold. For a holder of Japanese rate exposure, the distinction is between Ueda’s stated direction for policy and the unresolved choice of when to act. The testimony supplied evidence for the former and identified variables that could affect the latter. It supplied no market-implied path against which to measure a surprise (pp. 2–3).

questions.question: What would show that higher import prices are becoming a persistent domestic wage and price shock?
questions.detail: Ueda identifies both imported goods inflation and domestic wage pass-through, but gives no decomposition. For the timing of the next hike, examine the price changes of labour-intensive services alongside durable goods, wage settlements and measures of medium-term expectations. The Bank’s underlying-inflation releases, official CPI breakdowns and contemporary wage surveys would help establish whether pressure is spreading beyond items directly exposed to oil, chips and the yen.

questions.question: How much of the slowdown can households and firms absorb before financial conditions cease to look accommodative?
questions.detail: The testimony describes resilient consumption, high profits and rising investment while forecasting slower growth. A front-end rate exposure depends on whether that support survives higher import and construction costs. Compare real household incomes and consumption volumes with company investment plans, borrowing costs and loan demand. Official national accounts, business surveys and bank lending statistics would help distinguish shrinking real spending from nominal increases caused by prices.

questions.question: Which part of the AI impulse would matter most if overseas demand weakened?
questions.detail: AI demand supports Japanese exports but also contributes to semiconductor-related price increases. A reversal could weaken orders and relieve some durable-goods inflation on different schedules. To assess the balance for rates and cyclical exposures, compare export volumes and orders for equipment with import-price indices and domestic selling prices. Official trade releases and contemporary corporate disclosures would help trace changes in volumes separately from exchange-rate translation.
